we propose a novel way to perform iterative inference, which does not need to model an energy function linking output variables, and that we demonstrate that this approach is more accurate than CRF-based approaches.

(1) denoising autoencoder-based conditional score estimation is a promising alternative to CRFs for pixel-wise segmentation, (2) this is especially true when the conditional score is used to iteratively perform inference, (3) a corrupted feedforward model can be used to estimate a conditional score, and (4) this approach is not restricted to image segmentation, but can also be used for other structured prediction tasks.

we propose a new method for iterative inference that is based on the conditional score estimated from a conditional denoising network, and that this approach performs well in comparison with other methods on the task of image segmentation.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a new way to perform iterative inference, which is not any more constrained by the definition of an explicit energy function, and that this approach outperforms previous ones.
we have developed a new method for iterative inference from conditional scores, and applied it to image segmentation.

we propose to use a denoising autoencoder to learn a score function for the output variable given the input, which we then maximize in an iterative manner to find the most likely output given the input.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to perform efficient iterative inference from score estimation by denoisers, without having to explicitly define a parametric joint model of the output variables.

, in the absence of a good parametrization of the joint distribution of outputs, one can use a denoising autoencoder to learn the score of a distribution, and then use this estimated score to perform gradient ascent to find a local maximum of the distribution.

, when the joint distribution of outputs is complex, it is advantageous to use a conditional denoising model to estimate the conditional score, and then use this to perform gradient ascent to find a mode of the distribution.
